title: A Basis-Aware Approach to Quantum Sampling of the Fermi-Hubbard Ladder
authors: Adam Leicester, Zixu Wang, Jack Mandell, Yangyang Xu, Osama Muhammad Raisuddin, Haimeng Zhang, Jian Shi
abstract: Sample-based quantum diagonalization can reduce the classical cost of many-body calculations by restricting diagonalization to configurations identified through quantum sampling, but its efficiency depends on how compactly the target state is represented in the sampled basis. We investigate this dependence for sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization of the half-filled Fermi-Hubbard ladder using physically motivated one-body orbital rotations. Across position, momentum, bonding/antibonding, and leg-mode representations, the most compressible basis varies systematically with interaction strength and hopping anisotropy, with momentum sampling favored in the weakly interacting regime and geometry- or interaction-adapted representations becoming advantageous as the dominant energy scale changes. Near intermediate interaction and isotropic hopping, however, even the most favorable representation remains poorly compressible. Statevector SKQD calculations further show that basis choice strongly affects sampling efficiency. Hardware calculations on systems containing up to 120 qubits retain qualitative signatures of this basis dependence while revealing increasing particle-number leakage and reconstruction sensitivity with system size. These results show that scalable sample-based diagonalization requires co-design of the sampled representation, quantum circuit, and classical reconstruction procedure.
summary: This work analyzes the efficiency of quantum sampling techniques for simulating the Fermi-Hubbard ladder, demonstrating that the choice of basis representation is crucial for success. By comparing momentum, position, and bonding bases, the authors show that the best basis changes systematically with interaction parameters. Ultimately, they argue that realizing scalable quantum simulation requires a holistic co-design approach involving the basis, the quantum circuit, and the classical reconstruction method.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the choice of basis representation affects the efficiency of sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) for simulating strongly correlated electron systems.
main_result: The optimal basis for sampling is highly dependent on the interaction strength and hopping anisotropy, suggesting that scalable quantum simulation requires co-designing the basis, quantum circuit, and classical reconstruction procedure.
method: The authors compare various physically motivated one-body orbital rotations (e.g., momentum, bonding/antibonding) to determine which basis yields the most compressible representation of the ground-state wave function.
model_or_system: The primary model studied is the Fermi-Hubbard Ladder, a minimal system relevant to cuprate superconductors, described by a Hamiltonian involving hopping ($t$) and onsite repulsion ($U$).
key_observables: Compressibility (minimum basis size to retain 99% ground-state weight), relative energy error in statevector SKQD calculations, and two-qubit gate count/depth for hardware mapping.
important_parameters: Interaction strength ($U/t$), hopping anisotropy ($t_{	ext{rung}}/t_{	ext{leg}}$), and the specific basis used for sampling (position, momentum, etc.).
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that the target ground state is sufficiently compressible in the sampled basis; otherwise, the advantage of SQD is lost.
figures_summary: Figures compare Hamiltonian matrix structures in different bases, show the dependence of reconstruction error on the retained subspace fraction, and compare hardware overheads for different circuit mappings.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the basis dependence of SQD efficiency, comparing multiple physically motivated bases for the Fermi-Hubbard ladder, followed by detailed hardware overhead and reconstruction quality analyses.
why_interesting: The findings directly address the resource scaling and feasibility of quantum simulation for strongly correlated materials, providing critical guidelines for designing quantum algorithms for condensed matter physics.

Figure 3: Basis-dependent compressibility fW and size scaling of the half-filled Fermi-Hubbard ladder. (a) Most compressible representation across the sampled parameter space for a 12-site ladder at W ≥0.99. (b) Minimum required subspace fraction, with the open square marking the representative least-compressible point. (d) Subspace-size scaling for several cumulative-weight thresholds from the momentum basis, with dashed curves denoting extrapolation beyond the computed system sizes.
